summary:
Nayarit stands within Mexico's federal legal framework. A 2017 reform of the state Civil Code established an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, allowing adults to change identity documents to match their gender identity. The Human Rights Watch roundup of 31 March 2025 counts Nayarit among the 22 of Mexico's 32 states that have legislated such procedures, alongside eight states with none and two more that recognise it in practice without legislation; the same document records 2019 national Supreme Court guidelines and notes that only seven states extend recognition to children.

Nayarit is the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfemicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years in 2024. Mexico City followed in July 2024 as the second jurisdiction to do so, with up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law. The Nayarit measure also lets friends, not just relatives, identify and claim bodies and drive investigations, a provision relevant where families disown trans relatives. In 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, a figure believed to be higher for transfemicides.
tangentialFactors:
Nayarit's transfemicide statute places it ahead of every other Mexican state on this specific offence, but the surrounding impunity rate is national: more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022, and the rate for transfemicides is believed to be higher still. A statutory penalty therefore coexists with a low probability of conviction.

The state's 2017 recognition reform predates most of the national field, yet Human Rights Watch's March 2025 assessment still describes implementation across Mexico as uneven, with recognition absent or obstructed in some states exposing trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation in dealings with identity documents.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Nayarit can use the administrative procedure created by the 2017 Civil Code reform to change identity documents to match their gender identity. The procedure applies to adults; only seven of Mexico's 32 states extend recognition to children, and the sources do not state whether Nayarit is among them.

Nayarit's 2024 transfemicide law carries sentences of up to 60 years and permits friends as well as relatives to identify and claim bodies and push investigations forward, addressing cases where families disown a trans relative.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Nayarit's recognition procedure has documented delays, refusals or discriminatory handling in practice is unresolved in the sources; the inventory confirms the procedure exists but supplies no Nayarit-specific implementation findings.

Nayarit-specific data on killings of trans people, on police or prosecutorial handling of such cases, and on whether the 2024 transfemicide statute has been applied at least once are not sourced here.

Whether Nayarit extends legal gender recognition to children is not stated in the inventory and remains unresolved.
